title: Reserved Capacity Onboarding Playbook — SLA banding, load shapes, and GPU selection guidance
creator: Asha Patel
description: Create a repeatable onboarding playbook and rubric for enterprise reserved capacity requests. The playbook should map customer workload signals to an SLA banding scheme, recommend GPU families and sizing heuristics, and prescribe scaling/burst policies. Deliverables: intake questionnaire template, SLA tier definitions, GPU-selection guidance, and an engineer-ready runbook for Dedicated ops teams.
background: We continue to see enterprise customers requesting reserved capacity with widely varying workload characteristics (chat vs batch embeddings vs reranking). Current intake conversations are ad-hoc and often result in either overprovisioning (high cost) or underprovisioning (SLA misses). This ticket consolidates learnings from recent onboardings into a prescriptive playbook to standardize expectations, reduce iteration, and accelerate sales/SE handoffs.
scope:
- Intake questionnaire and gating rubric for enterprise sales/solutions engineering
- SLA band definitions (latency & availability) with corresponding throughput units and GPU classes
- GPU selection heuristics including quantization and KV-cache implications
- Recommended autoscaling & burst policies for reserved pools (pre-warm, sustained vs burst capacity, preemption guidance)
- Observable metrics & dashboards to validate post-onboarding SLA adherence
- Companion cost-estimation template for customer conversations
acceptance_criteria: Intake questionnaire accepted by Sales and Solutions Engineering
SLA banding matrix reviewed and approved by Runtime and Reliability teams
GPU selection guidance validated against three representative workloads (chat, embeddings, rerank) with benchmark numbers
Autoscaling policy examples implemented as config snippets for Dedicated autoscaler and tested in staging
Customer-facing onboarding checklist and internal runbook published (Confluence link)
sla_tiers: Tier A — Latency-critical: P95 < 60ms for streaming text gen, P99 < 250ms for non-streaming; availability SLA 99.95%; reserved throughput >= 250 tokens/s per 80GB GPU equivalent
Tier B — Interactive: P95 < 200ms streaming, P99 < 800ms non-streaming; availability SLA 99.9%; reserved throughput 50–250 tokens/s per GPU equivalent
Tier C — Throughput-first / batch: No hard tail-latency SLO; throughput SLA (jobs/hour) and completion time targets; availability SLA 99.5%; recommend batched nodes and cheaper quantized profiles
gpu_selection_guidelines: Baseline: map SLA tier to GPU family — Tier A: H100 80GB or equivalent; Tier B: A100 80GB or H100 40GB for mixed workloads; Tier C: 80-bit quantized A10/A30 or 4-bit quantized A100 depending on model compatibility
KV-cache-heavy chat: prioritize larger VRAM or multi-GPU shard due to KV residency — recommend 80GB class or split-sharded prompts with transparent fallback
Embeddings: prefer memory-optimized instances; use lower precision (fp16/4-bit) for cost efficiency when output quality tests pass
Quantization: include a 'quality gate' — run benchmark prompt set and check delta against baseline (ROUGE/BLEU or task-specific metrics) before approving quantized profile
Model variants: recommend pinned model versions and a compatible smaller variant for graceful degradation (e.g., quantized-1 -> quantized-2)
scaling_policies: Sustained vs burst separation: require customers to commit sustained throughput. Allow short bursts (configurable window e.g., 5 minutes) billed to reserved pool but subject to 'burst budget' limits
Pre-warm warming: for Tier A customers, include pre-warm policies (keep a fraction of nodes hot) with warmup runbooks for model weights and KV prefill

Autoscaling knobs: target CPU/GPU utilization, p99 latency, and queue length as triggers. Default conservative scale-up policy: add 1 node at 70% sustained GPU util or when queue depth exceeds 20 requests per node for >30s
Fallback routing: on capacity pressure route to compatible model variant (smaller quantized model) with explicit customer consent and visibility in console
Preemption and fairness: define preemption bands across customers in the same reserved pool; critical Tier A workloads should be isolated into dedicated sub-pools when possible
intake_questionnaire: https://confluence.redwood.ai/dedicated/onboarding/intake-template — includes workload profile, traffic pattern CSV example, target SLOs, model(s) to serve, preferred regions, data residency constraints, encryption/KMS requirements, and acceptable fallback behaviors
decisions: Use a three-band SLA scheme (A/B/C) to balance simplicity and fidelity — approved by PM and Runtime leads (2026-02-18)
Require a short benchmark run for ANY quantized recommendation (bench harness link provided) before changing GPU class — decision logged
Default burst window is 5 minutes with configurable budget; burst capacity billed against committed pool unless explicit burst purchases are made
Operationally require Solutions Engineering to attach a 'workload profile' artifact (traffic CSV + sample prompts) at intake to avoid repeated right-sizing cycles
open_questions: Should we mandate dedicated sub-pools for all Tier A customers or allow co-tenancy with strict isolation guardrails? (seeking SRE cost estimate)
How granular should billing for burst usage be represented on invoices? (Finance input needed)
Edge-case: handling multi-model routing where different models have incompatible quantization/precision — need a routing strategy and compatibility matrix
